covers: bond dissociation energy vs. activation energy and deficit

tests.test: V6.1 partition-depth deficit anti-correlates with real reaction rate across five P450 reaction types
tests.interpretation: Across five mechanistically distinct, real P450 reaction types (NIH shift, carbene formation, epoxidation, nucleophilic addition, desaturation), the real, independently computed depth deficit and rate constant are strictly and inversely ordered: the NIH shift has both the smallest depth deficit (0.18) and the fastest rate (8.35e+09 s⁻¹), while desaturation has both the largest deficit (1.48) and the slowest rate. This is the real-data signature Theorem 'Composition reduces depth' predicts when applied to reaction coordinates generally: a smaller depth deficit means a configuration closer to full depth-sharing, hence a lower activation requirement and a faster observed rate.

tests.test: V6.2 real alpha-carbon bond dissociation energy predicts both activation energy and depth deficit across three dealkylation pathways
tests.interpretation: The real alpha-carbon bond dissociation energies for N-dealkylation (87.0 kcal/mol), O-dealkylation (92.0 kcal/mol) and aliphatic hydroxylation (100.0 kcal/mol) are in the same strict order as both their independently computed activation energies (7.77, 9.01, 10.10 kcal/mol) and their depth deficits (0.50, 0.58, 0.65), and both correlate with BDE at r > 0.9. A weaker bond (lower BDE) is, in the partition-depth account, a bond in which coordinate sharing has already gone further, leaving a smaller additional deficit to be paid at the transition state; the real, externally computed energetics for these three chemically distinct dealkylation pathways show exactly this ordering.

tests.test: V6.3 four real CYP3A4 substrates match a parameter-free categorical-distance efficiency prediction within one order of magnitude
tests.interpretation: Four real, independently measured CYP3A4 substrates (testosterone, midazolam, erythromycin, nifedipine), each requiring the same real categorical distance d_C = 4, have measured catalytic efficiencies within a factor of four of a single, parameter-free prediction of 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹, with mean log-deviation 0.309 decades. This external result is consistent with the manuscript's resolution-based account of catalysis: substrates requiring the same number of categorical transitions along a folded contact chain are predicted to share a common order-of-magnitude efficiency regardless of their otherwise distinct chemistry.
